title: A King Who Only Half Listened
overview: King Amaziah of Judah starts out heeding God's warnings, but after a victory over Edom he grows proud, turns to foreign gods and brings disaster on himself and his kingdom.

parts.label: A good start, half-hearted (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Amaziah kept up the worship of the LORD, but the writer says his heart was not fully in it, which sets up everything that follows. He executed the men who murdered his father but spared their children, following the law of Moses that each person dies for their own wrong, unusual restraint when kings often wiped out whole families.

parts.label: Hired soldiers sent home (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: He bought the services of 100,000 soldiers from the northern kingdom of Israel, but a prophet warned that the LORD was not with them, since the north worshipped at shrines with golden calf images. Amaziah obeyed and lost the silver he had paid, and the prophet's answer was that God could give him far more than that.

parts.label: Victory and brutality (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: Judah defeated Edom (also called Seir) and then threw 10,000 captives off a cliff, a cruelty the text reports plainly without praising it. Meanwhile the dismissed soldiers, angry at losing their share of the loot, raided Judah's own towns and killed 3,000 people.

parts.label: Worshipping defeated gods (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Amaziah brought home the idols of the people he had just beaten and worshipped them, and a prophet asked the obvious question: why trust gods that could not even save their own people? The king threatened him into silence, and the prophet replied that God had now decided to destroy him.

parts.label: The thistle and the cedar (vv. 17-24)
parts.note: Puffed up by his win, Amaziah challenged Israel's King Jehoash, who answered with a mocking fable: a little thistle acting like the equal of a mighty cedar gets trampled, so stay home. Amaziah refused, was captured, Jerusalem's wall was broken down and the temple and palace treasures were carried off, which the writer sees as judgment for turning to Edom's gods.

parts.label: A violent end (vv. 25-28)
parts.note: He lived fifteen more years, but people in Jerusalem plotted against him from the time he turned away from the LORD. He fled to the town of Lachish and was killed there, then carried back and buried with the kings in Jerusalem.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read verse 20, which says God brought about Amaziah's refusal to listen: some see God actively steering him toward defeat, while others see God letting the king's own pride run its course.
think: Amaziah could accept a warning that cost him money but not one that hurt his pride, so why might advice be hardest to hear right after a success?
